Project proposal: Sleep duration and depressive symptoms in US adults

Hailin Cao

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

Research question

How is nightly sleep duration associated with depressive symptoms among US adults aged 20 and older?

Data and provenance

Dataset Source Content
NHANES (R package NHANES) CDC/NCHS National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009–2010 and 2011–2012 cycles 10,000 participants resampled from NHANESraw to approximate a simple random sample of the US population; 76 demographic, health, and lifestyle variables
NHANESraw (same package) Same surveys, original sample Includes survey weights (WTINT2YR, WTMEC2YR), PSU, and strata for design-based estimates

Unit of analysis and population

  • Unit: individual survey participant.
  • Population: US adults aged 20 and older, 2009–2012.

Exposure

  • Variable: SleepHrsNight, self-reported usual hours of sleep on weeknights or workdays (integer).
  • Coding: short (<6< 6 h), recommended (66–88 h, reference), and long (>8> 8 h). The app will let users move these cutoffs.
  • Missing data: participants missing SleepHrsNight are excluded from the primary complete-case analysis. The amount and pattern of missingness will be reported, and a sensitivity analysis will use multiple imputation (mice).

Outcome

  • Variable: Depressed, self-reported number of days in the past 2 weeks feeling down, depressed, or hopeless: None / Several / Most.
  • Type: ordinal categorical (three ordered levels). A binary version (None vs. Several/Most) will be used as a secondary outcome.

Confounders (chosen a priori)

  • Age and Gender: both are associated with sleep patterns and depression.
  • Race1: proxy for social and structural factors that affect sleep and mental health.
  • Poverty (income-to-poverty ratio): financial stress affects both sleep and mood.
  • PhysActive: may be a confounder, but could also be a mediator (sleep → activity → mood). The primary model includes it, and a sensitivity analysis drops it.

Anticipated limitations

  • Cross-sectional design: depression can disrupt sleep, so the direction of the association cannot be established (reverse causation).
  • Self-report: both sleep hours and depressive symptoms are self-reported and subject to recall and reporting bias.
  • Unmeasured confounding: e.g., chronic illness, medications, shift work.
  • Survey design: the resampled NHANES data approximate a simple random sample. Design-based estimates from NHANESraw with survey weights will be compared where feasible.

Planned deliverables

  1. Vignette: sleep and depression in NHANES. Data provenance, descriptive statistics, model results, findings, and limitations.

  2. Interactive Shiny app, stored in inst/shiny/ and launched with a package function run_app(). Users can:

    • choose an age range and the sleep cutoffs,
    • add or remove confounders and compare unadjusted vs. adjusted odds ratios,
    • view the distribution of depressive symptoms by sleep category.

    The app will be published with Shinylive in the pkgdown site, or on shinyapps.io and linked from the vignette.

    1. Second vignette: spatiotemporal patterns in US homicide mortality (cdcmurd, with cdcfiremort), updating the classic dslabs::murders examples.
      • Question: How did state homicide rates change from 2014 to 2024, and do states with higher firearm death rates also have higher homicide rates?
      • Data: CDC/NCHS State Statistics. cdcmurd gives the age-adjusted homicide rate per 100,000 (Death.Rate) and death counts by state, 2005 and 2014–2024; cdcfiremort gives the same measures for firearm deaths. The two tables are joined by state and year. cdcmurd uses postal abbreviations and cdcfiremort uses full state names, so they are matched via state.abb / state.name.
      • Unit: state-year (50 states + D.C., 2014–2024).
      • Limitations: ecological, state-level data; firearm deaths include suicides as well as homicides, so the two outcomes overlap; small states have less stable rates.
